title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Setup
Load the data first.
Code# Import data
hikes <- read.csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/high_peaks.csv")

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 1: Research Questions
Let’s dig into the hikes data, starting with the elevation and difficulty ratings of the hikes:

Codelibrary(tidyverse)
head(hikes)

             peak elevation difficulty ascent length time    rating
1     Mt. Marcy        5344          5   3166   14.8 10.0  moderate
2 Algonquin Peak       5114          5   2936    9.6  9.0  moderate
3   Mt. Haystack       4960          7   3570   17.8 12.0 difficult
4   Mt. Skylight       4926          7   4265   17.9 15.0 difficult
5 Whiteface Mtn.       4867          4   2535   10.4  8.5      easy
6       Dix Mtn.       4857          5   2800   13.2 10.0  moderate



What features would we like a visualization of the categorical difficulty rating variable to capture? It should show the categories and the number of hikes in each category, so we can compare in different difficulty level.
What about a visualization of the quantitative elevation variable? It should show the distribution of elevation values: the range, spread, shape of the distribution, and outliers.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 2: Load tidyverse
We’ll address the above questions using ggplot tools. Try running the following chunk and simply take note of the error message – this is one you’ll get a lot!

Code# Use the ggplot function
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating))







In order to use ggplot tools, we have to first load the tidyverse package in which they live. We’ve installed the package but we need to tell R when we want to use it. Run the chunk below to load the library. You’ll need to do this within any .qmd file that uses ggplot().

Code# Load the package
library(tidyverse)

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
section: Exercise 3: Bar Chart of Ratings - Part 1
text:
Exercise 3: Bar Chart of Ratings - Part 1
Consider some specific research questions about the difficulty rating of the hikes:

How many hikes fall into each category?
Are the hikes evenly distributed among these categories, or are some more common than others?

All of these questions can be answered with: (1) a bar chart; of (2) the categorical data recorded in the rating column. First, set up the plotting frame:

Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating))







Think about:

What did this do? What do you observe? Create a frame.
What, in general, is the first argument of the ggplot() function? Clarify the data set we want to visualize.
What is the purpose of writing x = rating? Put rating on x axis.
What do you think aes stands for?!? Aesthetics.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
section: Exercise 4: Bar Chart of Ratings - Part 2
text:
Exercise 4: Bar Chart of Ratings - Part 2
Now let’s add a geometric layer to the frame / canvas, and start customizing the plot’s theme. To this end, try each chunk below, one by one. In each chunk, make a comment about how both the code and the corresponding plot both changed.
NOTE:

Pay attention to the general code properties and structure, not memorization.
Not all of these are “good” plots. We’re just exploring ggplot.


Code# Add a "+" in the code. The plot get three bars and number on the y axis.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_bar()








Code# The code named the x and y axis, which shows on the graph.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Rating", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# The code add fill = "blue", thus the bars show in blue color.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "blue") +
  labs(x = "Rating", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# The code add color = "orange", then the line outside of the bar turns orange.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_bar(color = "orange", fill = "blue") +
  labs(x = "Rating", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# By adding theme_minimal() in the code, the plot's background turns in white color.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_bar(color = "orange", fill = "blue")  +
  labs(x = "Rating", y = "Number of hikes") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 5: Bar Chart Follow-up
Part a
Reflect on the ggplot() code.

What’s the purpose of the +? When do we use it? Add things on the plot.
We added the bars using geom_bar()? Why “geom”? Geometric.
What does labs() stand for? Labels?
What’s the difference between color and fill? Color changes the color of the outer line, while fill changes the color inside the bars.
Part b
In general, bar charts allow us to examine the following properties of a categorical variable:


observed categories: What categories did we observe? Difficult, easy, moderate.

variability between categories: Are observations evenly spread out among the categories, or are some categories more common than others? Moderate is more common than others.

We must then translate this information into the context of our analysis, here hikes in the Adirondacks. Summarize below what you learned from the bar chart, in context.
Part c
Is there anything you don’t like about this barplot? For example: check out the x-axis again.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 6: Sad Bar Chart
Let’s now consider some research questions related to the quantitative elevation variable:

Among the hikes, what’s the range of elevation and how are the hikes distributed within this range (eg, evenly, in clumps, “normally”)?
What’s a typical elevation?
Are there any outliers, ie, hikes that have unusually high or low elevations?

Here:

Construct a bar chart of the quantitative elevation variable.
Explain why this might not be an effective visualization for this and other quantitative variables. (What questions does / doesn’t it help answer?)


Code# write your code here
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "red")

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 7: A Histogram of Elevation
Quantitative variables require different viz than categorical variables. Especially when there are many possible outcomes of the quantitative variable. It’s typically insufficient to simply count up the number of times we’ve observed a particular outcome as the bar graph did above. It gives us a sense of ranges and typical outcomes, but not a good sense of how the observations are distributed across this range. We’ll explore two methods for graphing quantitative variables: histograms and density plots.
Histograms are constructed by (1) dividing up the observed range of the variable into ‘bins’ of equal width; and (2) counting up the number of cases that fall into each bin. Check out the example below:

Part a
Let’s dig into some details.

How many hikes have an elevation between 4500 and 4700 feet? 6
How many total hikes have an elevation of at least 5100 feet? 44
Part b
Now the bigger picture. In general, histograms allow us to examine the following properties of a quantitative variable:


typical outcome: Where’s the center of the data points? What’s typical? Around 4000.

variability & range: How spread out are the outcomes? What are the max and min outcomes? From 3700 to 5500.

shape: How are values distributed along the observed range? Is the distribution symmetric, right-skewed, left-skewed, bi-modal, or uniform (flat)? It’s roughly symmetric.

outliers: Are there any outliers, ie, outcomes that are unusually large/small? No obvious outliers.

We must then translate this information into the context of our analysis, here hikes in the Adirondacks. Addressing each of the features in the above list, summarize below what you learned from the histogram, in context.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 8: Building Histograms - Part 1
2-MINUTE CHALLENGE: Thinking of the bar chart code, try to intuit what line you can tack on to the below frame of elevation to add a histogram layer. Don’t forget a +. If it doesn’t come to you within 2 minutes, no problem – all will be revealed in the next exercise.

Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram()

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 9: Building Histograms - Part 2
Let’s build some histograms. Try each chunk below, one by one. In each chunk, make a comment about how both the code and the corresponding plot both changed.

Code# Changing geom_bar to geom_histogram, the plot's bar graph change to histogram.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram()








Code# The code adds color = "white", changing the outer line of each bin to white color.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white") 








Code# The code adds fill = "blue". The bins' color inside turns into blue.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "blue") 








Code# The code deletes fill = "blue", so the color of the bins turns grey. By adding labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes"), the plots x axis's name is Elevation(feet), y axis's name is Number of hikes.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# The code adds binwidth = 1000, so the plot only shows two bins with a width 1000.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 1000) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# The code changes binwidth to 5, thus there are many bins on the plot with a width of 5.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 5) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# The code changes binwidth to 200, thus there are 9 bins on the plot with a width of 200.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 200) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 10: Histogram Follow-up

What function added the histogram layer / geometry? geom_histogram()
What’s the difference between color and fill? Color: outer line. Fill: inside the bars.
Why does adding color = "white" improve the visualization? It can separate each bin, making it easier to read.
What did binwidth do? Sets the width of each bin along the x-axis.
Why does the histogram become ineffective if the binwidth is too big (eg, 1000 feet)? This will combine too many value in one bin.
Why does the histogram become ineffective if the binwidth is too small (eg, 5 feet)? This is hard to read.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 11: Density Plots
Density plots are essentially smooth versions of the histogram. Instead of sorting observations into discrete bins, the “density” of observations is calculated across the entire range of outcomes. The greater the number of observations, the greater the density! The density is then scaled so that the area under the density curve always equals 1 and the area under any fraction of the curve represents the fraction of cases that lie in that range.
Check out a density plot of elevation. Notice that the y-axis (density) has no contextual interpretation – it’s a relative measure. The higher the density, the more common are elevations in that range.

Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_density()







Questions


INTUITION CHECK: Before tweaking the code and thinking back to geom_bar() and geom_histogram(), how do you anticipate the following code will change the plot?


geom_density(color = "blue") turns the outer line to blue.

geom_density(fill = "orange") turns the space under the line to orange.


TRY IT! Test out those lines in the chunk below. Was your intuition correct?


Code# Write your code here
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_density(color = "blue", fill = "orange")








Examine the density plot. How does it compare to the histogram? What does it tell you about the typical elevation, variability / range in elevations, and shape of the distribution of elevations within this range? The histogram uses bins to display counts of hikes at different elevations, while the density plot creates a smooth curve showing relative density. The horizontal spread of the curve reveals the range of elevation values, and the overall curve shape tells us whether the elevation distribution is.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 12: Density Plots vs Histograms
The histogram and density plot both allow us to visualize the behavior of a quantitative variable: typical outcome, variability / range, shape, and outliers. What are the pros/cons of each? What do you like/not like about each? The histogram shows counts of each bin. (like) The histogram cannot show an overall smooth trend. (not like) The density plot shows a smooth curth of the distribution. (like) The density plot cannot let people easily read how many observations there is. (not like)

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 13: Code = communication
We obviously won’t be done until we talk about communication. All code above has a similar general structure (where the details can change):

Codeggplot(___, aes(x = ___)) + 
  geom___(color = "___", fill = "___") + 
  labs(x = "___", y = "___")



Though not necessary to the code working, it’s common, good practice to indent or tab the lines of code after the first line (counterexample below). Why? Because to indent or tab the lines of code after the first line can help people read the code, which is more tidy.


Code# YUCK
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 200) +
labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Though not necessary to the code working, it’s common, good practice to put a line break after each + (counterexample below). Why? Also as a better way to read the code.


Code# YUCK 
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) + geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 200) + labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")
